chunks.text: TL;DR
Most independent restaurants rebuild their website 12–24 months later than they should — when the cost is higher and the funnel is already leaking.
A seven-question diagnostic separates "rebuild" from "fix the leaks for another year" without a consultant in the loop.

Three case patterns: a high-scoring site that just needs targeted fixes; a sub-60 site where the platform itself is the ceiling; a mid-range site where a partial rebuild is the right cost-benefit trade.
The decision is rarely "rebuild or not." It is "what level of rebuild, and what does the 18-month do-nothing case look like."

The conversation almost always starts the same way: an operator has two quotes for a rebuild that differ by 3-4x, neither developer has asked what is actually broken, and the operator is not really asking which quote to take. They are asking whether to rebuild at all. That is the harder question, and almost nobody helps operators answer it.

The honest answer is that most independent restaurants rebuild 12-24 months later than they should — by which time the rebuild costs more (because there is more to migrate), takes longer (because the bookings funnel has gotten worse), and the operator is making the decision under stress instead of under planning.
This is the seven-question diagnostic I run through before recommending a rebuild — or, just as often, recommending against one and pointing at three small changes that buy another year.

Storefront Health score · what it tells you about rebuild readiness. Do not rebuild: Fix the lowest sub-score. Sometimes a C D N + image pass earns another year. (fix leaks). Maybe rebuild: Walk through the seven questions — three or more "yes" = rebuild. (diagnose). Rebuild: Every quarter you wait costs more than the rebuild itself. (rebuild now). Storefront Health score · what it tells you about rebuild readiness.
Question 1: How does it score on Storefront Health?
Run Storefront Health on your site. The composite scorecard rolls speed, S E O, mobile, schema, G B P, and the Restaurant Audit into one number, 0-100.
80+: Do not rebuild. Fix the lowest sub-score.
60-79: Maybe rebuild. Read the next six questions.
Below 60: Rebuild — every quarter you wait costs more than the rebuild.
Question 2: Can your C M S update without breaking the site?

Old C M S installs accumulate technical debt the way ductwork accumulates dust. The test: when's the last time someone tried to update the platform? If the answer is "we do not, because it broke last time," that is a rebuild signal.
Question 3: Does the menu live in H T M L?

If your menu is a P D F, an image, or "managed by Wix's menu widget," you are invisible to Google's dish-level queries and to AI search. Switching to a real H T M L menu alone is sometimes enough to defer a rebuild — sometimes it requires one.
Question 4: How does the site score on Core Web Vitals?

If LCP is above 4 seconds on mobile, or CLS is above 0.25, you are being penalized in search AND bouncing visitors before the menu loads. Sometimes a C D N + image compression fixes it; sometimes the platform is the problem and only a rebuild will do.

Run Speed Test on the homepage and the busiest interior page. If the homepage is fast but the menu page is slow, the platform is not the issue — the page is. If both are slow, the platform usually is.
Question 5: Can you ship a small change in under an hour?

Test: try to update the holiday hours on your homepage in the next 60 minutes. If you cannot (no access, complex C M S, requires a developer), that is a rebuild signal — not because the technical limitation is fatal, but because the operational burden compounds quietly. Every change you delay is a small leak.
Question 6: Does the brand match the room?

Open your homepage on the phone you carry. Then walk into your dining room. Do they feel like the same place? If not — if the room is warm, considered, intentional, and the site is templated, generic, "we picked the cleanest Squarespace template" — that is a brand-design rebuild signal, separate from the technical ones.
Question 7: What happens to bookings if you do nothing for 18 months?

Look at your monthly booking trend. If it is flat or declining and your site has been the same for 24+ months, doing nothing is not actually neutral — the gap to your local competitors is widening even when your numbers look stable. The 18-month "do nothing" projection is almost always negative for a stale restaurant site.

Three rebuild patterns · score band, scope, typical payback. High-scoring site, targeted fixes: Score 75–85. C D N, compress, schema fix. ~5–10% of rebuild cost. (defer). Sub-60 site, full rebuild: Platform itself caps the ceiling. Real H T M L menu, full schema, fast funnel. (9–14 mo payback). Mid-range, partial rebuild: Front-end + photos, keep C M S. ~40% of full-rebuild cost. Watch the ceiling. (tradeoff). Three rebuild patterns · score band, scope, typical payback.
Three case threads.

Case 1 — Bistro on a 75 score, does not rebuild: A six-year-old French bistro scoring 75 on Storefront Health. Mobile speed dragging the score down. We added a C D N, recompressed every image, fixed the menu schema. Score moved to 88; they deferred the rebuild for two more years and saved roughly 11 dollarsK.

Case 2 — Site below 60, rebuilds: Old front-end, slow on mobile, menu schema malformed, booking funnel hidden. The platform itself is the ceiling. The rebuild here is full custom: real H T M L menu, dish-level structured data, the booking funnel cleaned up. Score lands in the high 80s or 90s. Search-driven reservations roughly triple within 90 days because the missing schema starts firing in local-pack queries the site never appeared for before. Payback windows on rebuilds in this range are typically 9-14 months — but the leverage compounds as Google's index updates.

Case 3 — Site at 65-70, partial rebuild: Platform fine, brand tired. Keep the C M S, replace the front-end and the photos at roughly 40% of a full-rebuild cost. Score moves into the low-mid 80s. Bookings tick up — but not as steeply as Case 2. The honest tradeoff worth flagging: a partial rebuild caps your ceiling at whatever the underlying platform allows for schema, speed, and indexing. Sometimes the right call; sometimes worth revisiting in 18 months when the platform's ceiling becomes the next constraint.
Doing nothing is not neutral. The gap to your local competitors widens every quarter your site does not.
How to use this framework.

Run Storefront Health first. Save the score to your Workshop . Walk through the seven questions, write down the honest answer to each, and look at the pattern. If three or more are pointing at "rebuild," you are past due. If one or two are, you are in fix-the-leak territory — read Five Website Changes That Recover 1% Margin for the targeted-fix approach.
If you want a second pair of eyes on the framework as it applies to your site, write through The Window . I read every one.
Key takeaways
Run Storefront Health first. Sub-60 = rebuild now. 60–79 = walk through the seven questions. 80+ = fix the lowest sub-score.
C M S that cannot update without breaking is a rebuild signal — accumulating debt compounds.
P D F or widget-locked menus cap your indexability. Sometimes a menu rewrite alone defers a rebuild a year.
If you cannot ship a small change in under an hour, the operational burden is already a leak.
Doing nothing is not neutral. The gap to local competitors widens every quarter your site does not.
Get the score before you make the call.

Storefront Health is a free composite scorecard that rolls speed, S E O, mobile, schema, and G B P into one number 0–100. The decision framework above only works once you have the score. Run it now and save it to your Workshop.
